# Meaning as a cognitive representation

<p>My research investigates how meaning is represented and used in the mind: what form those representations take, how they are constructed, enriched, and inferred during comprehension, and how they are encoded, organized, and retrieved from memory.</p>

<p>My approach brings linguistic theory and experimental psycholinguistics together. Linguistic theory provides explicit hypotheses about how meaningful representations are structured; psycholinguistic theory provides hypotheses about the cognitive processes that construct and use those representations. Empirical evidence tests the predictions that follow from both, providing complementary constraints on theories of meaning and cognition.</p>

:::

<div class="selected-list">

::: {.selected-item}
**Thematic separation in light of sentence comprehension**  
Husband, E. M. · *Language and Linguistic Compass* · 2023

What does the grammatical representation of thematic relations commit us to about the processes that construct sentence meaning?

[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1111/lnc3.12496)
:::

::: {.selected-item}
**Nothing much for kinds**  
Husband, E. M. · *For Hagit: A celebration* · 2022

How is the kind/object distinction shaped by grammatical representation?
:::

::: {.selected-item}
**Relating word prediction and probability judgment: Online and offline probabilistic processes are partially shared**  
Zhang, Y. & Husband, E. M. · *Proceedings of the Cognitive Science Society* · 2026

Do our explicit judgments about what is probable and our moment-to-moment expectations during comprehension draw on the same probabilistic representations and processes?

[Paper](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/113553v6)
:::

::: {.selected-item}
**The impact of implicit scalar alternatives on the products of language comprehension: Evidence from recognition memory**  
Patson, N. & Husband, E. M. · *Memory & Cognition* · 2026

When comprehension makes implicit alternatives available, do those alternatives become part of the representation that persists in memory?

[DOI](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-026-01856-8)
:::

::: {.selected-item}
**An incremental QUD approach to causal discourse expectations**  
Yao, R., Altshuler, D. & Husband, E. M. · *Acta Psychologica* · 2026

Can comprehenders' expectations about what comes next be explained by the questions that become relevant as a discourse evolves?

[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2026.107670)
:::

::: {.selected-item}
**Speaking of death**  
Husband, E. M. · *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences* · 2018

What does the way events are grammatically encoded tell us about how events themselves are represented in the mind?

[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2018.0172)
:::

</div>

## DPhil students and postdocs
</div>

<a class="section-action" href="people.qmd">Information about working with me <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a>
:::

<div class="prospective-wide">
<p>I welcome enquiries from prospective DPhil students and postdoctoral researchers interested in meaning and cognition, particularly projects that connect questions about linguistic representation with questions about processing, inference, memory, or knowledge. I am especially interested in work that uses linguistic theory and experimental evidence to constrain one another.</p>

<p>Your project need not fall neatly within one of my current research topics. I am most interested in supervising work driven by a clear theoretical question about how meaning is represented, constructed, or used.</p>
</div>
